Build a production-ready distributed trace viewer for the existing TypeScript/React developer console. Ingest OpenTelemetry spans through the Node API, normalize them, persist searchable trace metadata in PostgreSQL, and render a virtualized waterfall with service, duration, error, and parent-child filtering. Add APIs, pagination, time-range queries, permissions, loading and error states, and URL-shareable selections. Preserve current authentication and public interfaces, support traces with 100k spans, and add unit, integration, and browser tests. Acceptance: seeded traces render correctly, filters and deep links survive reloads, access control is enforced, and CI passes.

Add screenshot-regression testing to the existing TypeScript/React developer-tools monorepo. Create a Playwright-based runner that captures stable Chromium screenshots across configured viewport and device profiles, masks dynamic regions, stores baselines and metadata, and produces an HTML diff report with pixel thresholds. Add CLI commands and CI integration for update and approve workflows, parallel execution, artifact retention, and pull-request annotations. Do not require a cloud service. Acceptance: deterministic sample tests pass on macOS and Linux, intentional changes fail with actionable diffs, baseline updates are reviewable, and unit, integration, and browser coverage protects the runner and report format.

Create a browser bridge for the existing Rust/TypeScript devtools suite using Chrome DevTools Protocol and Playwright. It must launch or attach to Chromium, manage multiple tabs and targets, stream console, network, and runtime events, execute typed commands, and recover from disconnects without leaking processes. Add a versioned message protocol, capability negotiation, structured errors, logging, and an adapter boundary for Firefox later; do not couple UI code to CDP details. Acceptance: parallel sessions work, reconnect tests pass, security blocks arbitrary host access, and end-to-end tests cover navigation, events, and shutdown.

Implement a plugin subsystem and private marketplace for the existing TypeScript developer-tools application. Define a versioned manifest and permission model, add plugin discovery through a registry proxy, install, uninstall, update, rollback, signature verification, and compatibility checks, and expose a management UI with progress and failure recovery. Plugins must run out of process or in a restricted sandbox and must not access credentials or arbitrary files without explicit grants. Provide migration handling for the current extension format, mock registry fixtures, and comprehensive API, security, and browser tests. Acceptance: approved plugins install reproducibly, denied permissions are enforced, upgrades can roll back, and offline use remains functional.

Build persistent terminal sessions for the existing Electron/TypeScript devtools app, backed by a Rust PTY helper. Support multiple tabs, resize and reconnect, UTF-8 streaming, searchable scrollback, exit status, environment profiles, cancellation, and bounded retention after restart. Keep shell execution behind the existing workspace permission model and prevent input/output cross-talk between sessions. Add IPC contracts, lifecycle telemetry, and unit, integration, and Electron tests. Acceptance: 50 concurrent sessions remain responsive, reconnect preserves output, shutdown cleans child processes, and CI covers Unix signal, shell startup, and malformed-output failure paths.

Build a coverage explorer for the existing TypeScript/Node developer-tools platform. Ingest Istanbul, LCOV, and Python coverage reports into a normalized model, persist runs and commit metadata, and provide APIs plus a virtualized source-tree and editor view with line heatmaps, branch details, filters, and diff coverage. Add historical trend charts, caching, partial-report handling, and clear stale-data indicators without slowing normal test runs. Preserve the current artifact format and authentication. Acceptance: fixtures from all supported formats produce equivalent results, large repositories remain responsive, diff coverage matches the CLI, and unit, integration, and browser tests pass.

Implement full Debug Adapter Protocol support in the existing TypeScript/Rust developer IDE. Add launch and attach configurations, process lifecycle management, breakpoints including conditions and logpoints, stepping, call stacks, scopes, variables, watches, exception filters, source maps, and multi-process events. Define a stable adapter interface so local and remote debuggers share the same UI state model, and preserve existing terminal behavior. Include configuration validation, cancellation, timeout handling, telemetry, and mock adapters. Acceptance: Node and Rust sample programs debug end to end, reconnects do not orphan processes, UI state survives reloads, and protocol, integration, and browser tests cover failure cases.

Build an incremental workspace indexer for the existing TypeScript/Node developer-tools workspace. Use tree-sitter parsers to extract symbols, imports, references, and diagnostics across the supported languages, honor gitignore and project configuration, watch file changes, and persist a versioned index for fast navigation and search. Indexing must be cancellable, bounded in memory, and isolated from the UI thread; expose progress and stale-state information through the current RPC layer. Acceptance: cold and incremental indexing are deterministic, edits update only affected files, corrupted indexes rebuild safely, cross-file queries return correct locations, and performance tests cover a million-line fixture.

Add HTTP and WebSocket record/replay support to the existing Go/TypeScript network devtools. Capture requests, responses, headers, timing, redirects, and WebSocket frames into a versioned archive, redact configurable secrets before persistence, and match replay traffic using method, URL, headers, and body rules with clear mismatch diagnostics. Provide a CLI, UI controls, import/export, retention limits, and deterministic virtual time for tests. Keep replay isolated from production credentials and support concurrent sessions. Acceptance: HAR fixtures round-trip, reordered or missing requests fail explainably, redaction is verified before disk writes, and integration tests cover redirects, streaming, WebSockets, and restart recovery.

Add remote development environment support to the existing Rust/TypeScript devtools application. Implement provider abstractions for SSH hosts and Docker-based containers, credential handoff without storing secrets, workspace mounting or synchronization, port forwarding, remote command execution, logs, health checks, reconnect, and explicit teardown. Expose environment creation and lifecycle state in the UI and preserve local workflows when no remote target is configured. Add quotas, cancellation, audit events, and failure recovery for interrupted provisioning. Acceptance: a sample project can build and debug remotely, forwarded services are reachable, reconnect restores sessions, cleanup leaves no orphan containers, and integration tests use disposable fixtures.

Create a flaky-test triage subsystem for the existing Python/TypeScript CI dashboard. Ingest historical test outcomes, retries, durations, commits, and environment metadata; calculate a transparent flakiness score; group related failures; and show ownership, trends, suspected causes, and quarantine status. Add APIs, scheduled aggregation, pagination, filters, export, and links back to CI artifacts. Triage actions must be permissioned, auditable, reversible, and compatible with the current test-result schema. Acceptance: seeded histories produce explainable rankings, incremental ingestion is idempotent, quarantine changes propagate to CI configuration, dashboard queries remain fast at scale, and unit, API, and browser tests cover edge cases.

Redesign the command palette as a shared subsystem for the existing TypeScript developer-tools suite. Create a typed command registry with plugin contribution points, context-aware enablement, fuzzy search, categories, recent history, keyboard navigation, nested actions, asynchronous commands, cancellation, and keybinding conflict resolution. Preserve existing shortcuts, expose accessible ARIA behavior, and prevent commands from bypassing workspace permissions. Add telemetry with privacy-safe event fields, a migration path for current ad hoc actions, and reusable UI and service packages. Acceptance: commands from core and plugins appear consistently, disabled reasons are discoverable, keyboard-only flows work, long-running actions remain cancellable, and unit, integration, accessibility, and browser tests pass.

Refactor the Python ingestion subsystem that consumes Kafka topics and partner REST feeds, lands raw data in S3, and registers datasets in Glue. Replace connector-specific control flow with a configuration-driven interface, shared retries and backoff, idempotency keys, dead-letter handling, and structured metrics. Preserve existing S3 layouts and downstream schemas during a staged migration, and support replay by date range. Add unit, contract, and local integration tests. Acceptance: all current connectors use the new interface, replay is deterministic, failures are observable, and CI passes without changing consumer-visible data.

Refactor the Airflow 2.8 DAG subsystem in Python: extract repeated scheduling, sensor, retry, and notification logic into tested shared operators and a small configuration layer. Preserve DAG IDs, task IDs, ownership metadata, SLAs, and historical backfill behavior while converting high-volume pipelines to dynamic task mapping where safe. Keep deployments compatible with the existing KubernetesExecutor and Postgres metadata database. Acceptance: no duplicate business logic remains across target DAGs, paused and running state survives deployment, backfills produce equivalent partitions, and unit plus integration tests cover retries, skips, and failures.

Refactor the Scala Spark Structured Streaming deduplication stage reading Kafka and writing Delta Lake. Define a single event identity and watermark policy, handle late and out-of-order records, bound state with configurable TTL, and make replay behavior deterministic. Preserve current output columns and checkpoint compatibility or provide an explicit migration path. Add metrics for duplicate rate, lateness, state size, and quarantined records, plus fixture-based and multi-hour integration tests. Acceptance: duplicate events are removed exactly once per configured key and window, restarts do not re-emit data, and load tests meet current throughput.

Rework the Kafka event-routing subsystem in Go that assigns events to downstream topics and partitions. Replace producer-specific partition rules with a versioned routing contract using consistent hashing, explicit tenant isolation, and a compatibility mode for existing keys. Coordinate changes across producers, the router, and consumers without losing ordering guarantees within a key. Add replay tooling, metrics for skew and unroutable events, and contract tests. Acceptance: old and new clients can run together, partition assignments are stable, no tenant crosses boundaries, and production-sized tests demonstrate bounded rebalance impact.

Unify the Python ETL execution paths currently split between Airflow tasks, Kubernetes Jobs, and a developer CLI. Design one runner API for configuration loading, secrets, retries, logging, cancellation, and exit status, then migrate representative batch and incremental pipelines without changing their outputs. Keep Kubernetes as the runtime and retain Airflow scheduling as an adapter. Provide a compatibility shim for existing command invocations, unit tests for lifecycle states, and end-to-end tests. Acceptance: all target pipelines use the same runner, failures are resumable, logs correlate by run ID, and old schedules still execute.

Refactor the Python backfill scripts that read partitioned Parquet from S3 and write to PostgreSQL and Snowflake into a resumable backfill service. Define a job manifest with source range, transform version, destination, and dependencies; add dry-run planning, checkpointed progress, bounded concurrency, rate limits, and safe retries. Preserve historical results and support pausing or restarting a job after partial failure. Include CLI and API entry points, audit records, and tests with injected failures. Acceptance: rerunning a completed range is idempotent, progress is queryable, and multi-day backfills resume without duplicate loads.

Refactor the Java Kafka Streams schema-evolution layer using Avro and Confluent Schema Registry. Centralize compatibility rules, version negotiation, default handling, and conversion adapters instead of duplicating them in each topology. Support rolling deployment across at least two schema versions, quarantine incompatible records with actionable metadata, and expose producer and consumer contract checks in CI. Preserve existing topic names and key formats, and document the migration sequence. Acceptance: backward and forward compatibility is enforced automatically, old consumers continue during rollout, bad records never halt the topology, and replay tests produce equivalent canonical events.

Refactor the Python batch-export subsystem that reads curated tables from BigQuery, writes encrypted Parquet to S3, and delivers files to client-specific prefixes. Replace one-off scripts with declarative export definitions and shared planning, partitioning, manifest, retry, and atomic-publish components. Preserve client schemas, naming conventions, retention rules, and KMS encryption. Add dry runs, resumable execution, row-count and checksum validation, and notifications. Acceptance: every migrated export has an auditable manifest, partial files are never advertised as complete, reruns are idempotent, and integration tests cover schema drift and delivery failures.

Refactor the dbt and Great Expectations data-quality layer for the warehouse pipelines. Introduce a common check model with dataset, partition, severity, owner, and remediation metadata; remove duplicated SQL assertions; and separate blocking checks from informational profiling. Run checks incrementally in Airflow, persist results for trend queries, and route failures to the existing alerting channel. Do not change business transformations or silently downgrade current failures. Acceptance: all critical datasets use the shared model, historical results remain queryable, retries are safe, and CI validates check configuration plus representative failure cases.

Overhaul the Scala Spark 3.5 batch pipeline that transforms raw events into Apache Iceberg tables on S3. Separate extraction, transformation, validation, and commit boundaries; make configuration explicit; and support both full rebuilds and partition-incremental runs. Preserve table names, schemas, and audit columns while adding atomic commits, bad-record quarantine, and metrics for input and output counts. Keep compatibility with the existing EMR runtime and avoid a full rewrite of business logic. Acceptance: golden-data tests match current results, retries do not duplicate files, incremental runs are restartable, and benchmark throughput is no worse than today.

Refactor the Python and Snowflake warehouse-load subsystem that stages CSV and Parquet drops, validates schemas, and merges into dimensional tables. Replace table-specific loader branches with a metadata-driven load contract covering keys, column mapping, null policy, watermark, and merge strategy. Preserve existing history semantics and support schema additions without destructive changes. Add transactional staging, idempotent retries, drift quarantine, and structured load metrics. Acceptance: all priority tables use the contract, rerunning a batch yields the same rows, failed loads leave no partial merge, and reconciliation tests match source counts and checksums.

Refactor the Java Debezium and Kafka CDC processing pipeline that converts MySQL and Postgres change events into canonical records for Elasticsearch and the warehouse. Introduce a shared envelope for inserts, updates, deletes, tombstones, source positions, and transaction metadata; isolate connector-specific parsing; and define ordering and replay rules. Preserve existing topic contracts through versioned adapters, support resuming from offsets, and quarantine malformed events without stopping consumers. Acceptance: both sources pass golden replay tests, deletes and out-of-order transactions are handled consistently, lag and quarantine metrics exist, and rolling deployment causes no data loss.

In the Python Typer CLI, add pytest coverage for the existing config subcommand. Exercise loading defaults, a user-supplied YAML path, environment-variable overrides, and the error shown for malformed YAML. Keep tests isolated with tmp_path and monkeypatch; do not touch the real home directory or network. Reuse current fixtures and preserve the public command syntax. Acceptance: the repository’s normal pytest command passes, both success and failure paths are covered, and the tests fail if precedence changes from CLI flags over environment over file over defaults.

For the existing TypeScript Commander release CLI, write Vitest tests for the release command’s dry-run behavior. Cover semver validation, refusal when the working tree is dirty, and a successful plan without spawning git or publishing packages. Mock the process runner and filesystem through the project’s existing seams; keep snapshots limited to stable text. Acceptance: npm test passes, exit codes and key output are asserted, external commands and network are never invoked, and no temporary files remain.

In the Go Cobra CLI, add table-driven tests for the cache clean subcommand. Verify the default retention period, an explicit --older-than duration, dry-run output, and a missing-cache-directory case. Use t.TempDir and inject the clock and filesystem rather than reading the user’s cache or current time. Preserve existing exit-code conventions and output wording. Acceptance: go test ./... passes, tests cover deletion and no-op paths, and the suite proves dry-run never removes entries.

For the Rust clap CLI, add integration tests around shell-completion generation. Test bash, zsh, and fish as supported values, reject an unknown shell with a nonzero status, and verify generated output contains the registered top-level commands. Invoke the compiled binary through assert_cmd and keep assertions resilient to clap-version formatting. Acceptance: cargo test passes offline, tests do not write outside a temporary directory, and adding a command makes the completion test observe it.

In the Python argparse import CLI, write pytest tests for validation failures and partial-import behavior. Cover a missing input file, unsupported extension, duplicate record ID, and --continue-on-error. Build fixtures with tmp_path and monkeypatch the record store so no real database is used. Assert the structured error summary, exit status, and that valid rows commit only when continuation is enabled. Acceptance: pytest passes without network or database access and the tests protect the documented flags.

In the Node.js oclif CLI, add tests for the --verbose and --json output modes of the existing status command. Verify default human-readable output stays quiet, verbose mode includes diagnostic logger lines, and JSON mode emits parseable JSON without ANSI color codes. Stub the logger and status provider using the repository’s existing test seams. Acceptance: the normal npm test script passes, each mode asserts its exit code and key fields, and tests do not depend on terminal width, environment variables, or network access.

For the Go Cobra deploy command, add unit tests for the guarded deployment flow. Cover missing credentials, --plan mode, an explicit confirmation refusal, and a successful deployment response. Replace the API client, prompt, and command runner with fakes; do not contact a real service or invoke a shell. Preserve current messages and exit statuses. Acceptance: go test ./... passes, the success case verifies the request payload, refusal prevents any API call, and plan mode never mutates remote state.

In the Rust clap upload CLI, write tests for retry and backoff decisions. Use a deterministic fake HTTP transport and injected sleeper so the suite performs no real waits or network requests. Cover a transient 503 that succeeds on the third attempt, an immediate 4xx failure with no retry, and exhaustion after the configured limit. Assert attempt count, final status, and error text. Acceptance: cargo test --offline passes and the tests prove backoff is requested only between retryable attempts.

For the Python Click CLI, add parametrized tests for the report command’s format flags. Cover the default table output, JSON and CSV formats, the short alias, an unknown format, and combining --quiet with a valid format. Use in-memory fixtures and capsys; avoid filesystem, network, and locale dependence. Acceptance: pytest passes, each valid mode has a stable representative assertion, invalid input returns the documented nonzero code, and quiet mode suppresses progress output without changing report data.

In the TypeScript Commander CLI, add integration tests for failures from the command dispatcher. Exercise an unknown subcommand, a missing required argument, a handler-thrown operational error, and a successful invocation. Run the CLI through the project’s existing test harness with injected handlers so tests do not spawn unrelated processes or call services. Assert stderr versus stdout, exit codes, and the single user-facing error line. Acceptance: npm test passes and the tests preserve the current help and error conventions.

For the Go Cobra CLI, add golden-file tests for the root help and the config subcommand help. Generate output through the real command tree, but inject a deterministic terminal width and disable color so snapshots are stable. Include the usage line, available flags, and subcommands while avoiding timestamps or absolute paths. Acceptance: go test ./... passes, golden updates require an explicit test flag, and the snapshots fail when a documented command or flag disappears.

In the Python Typer CLI, add tests for graceful Ctrl-C handling in the watch command. Use a fake event source and injectable cleanup callback to simulate KeyboardInterrupt without sending signals to the test runner. Verify the command exits with the documented status, prints one concise cancellation message, and always closes the source on both interruption and normal completion. Acceptance: pytest passes without sleeping or starting threads, cleanup runs exactly once, and existing non-interactive behavior remains unchanged.

Refactor the Python/Django LMS monolith into independently deployable modules, extracting enrollment, course catalog, assignments, and gradebook behind versioned REST/gRPC interfaces while keeping the React web client behavior unchanged. Use PostgreSQL during the transition, Kafka for durable domain events, and an anti-corruption layer for legacy calls. Preserve permissions, audit history, retries, and existing API contracts; require no data loss or downtime during cutover. Acceptance: contract and end-to-end tests pass, dual writes reconcile, replayed events are idempotent, services deploy separately in Kubernetes, and documented rollback procedures work.

Refactor the Scala/Akka grading pipeline into versioned stages for submission ingestion, rubric execution, human moderation, and grade publication. Keep Kafka and PostgreSQL as durable sources of truth, add deterministic worker replay, and isolate institution-specific policies behind interfaces. Existing scores, late-work rules, partial-credit behavior, and audit trails must remain identical; historical submissions cannot be recomputed silently. Acceptance: golden fixtures match current results, at-least-once delivery produces no duplicate grades, failed jobs resume safely, throughput meets current peak plus 3x headroom, and operations can roll back by cohort.

Refactor the monolithic student identity layer in Java/Spring Boot around OIDC, SCIM, and a Keycloak-compatible provider, while preserving the public TypeScript client and existing school SSO links. Separate authentication, roster provisioning, account linking, consent, and authorization policy; support FERPA-sensitive audit retention and encrypted PII. Do not force password resets or change student IDs. Acceptance: Google, Microsoft, Clever, and SAML districts pass end-to-end tests; token rotation and revocation work; migration is resumable; legacy and new paths run in parallel; security, load, and rollback tests are documented.

Refactor the TypeScript/Node.js course-content subsystem into bounded authoring, versioning, publishing, and rendering modules with a stable GraphQL contract. Keep PostgreSQL metadata and S3-compatible assets, preserve immutable version IDs, SCORM packages, embedded media, and instructor permissions, and support draft/publish rollback without breaking active classes. Replace shared mutable models with explicit domain services and events. Acceptance: every existing course renders byte-for-byte where applicable, publishing remains atomic, concurrent edits do not lose content, migration handles millions of assets, and contract, accessibility, and end-to-end tests pass.

Refactor the Python event-analytics platform from ad hoc cron jobs into a governed Kafka-to-Spark pipeline with dbt models in Snowflake. Define a canonical learner-event schema, schema evolution rules, late-arrival handling, deduplication, and replayable backfills; preserve existing warehouse tables and dashboard metrics during a staged migration. PII must be minimized, encrypted, and access-controlled by institution. Acceptance: historical metrics reconcile within agreed tolerances, events are traceable to source, replays are idempotent, freshness meets the current SLA, and old jobs can be retired only after parallel-run signoff.

Refactor the Ruby on Rails/Sidekiq notification code into a shared delivery service covering email, SMS, push, and in-app messages for students, guardians, and staff. Centralize templates, localization, opt-outs, quiet hours, provider failover, deduplication, and tenant branding without changing enrollment or grade event semantics. Keep PostgreSQL records and existing provider credentials during migration, with an outbox for reliable dispatch. Acceptance: every existing notification has parity fixtures, retries are idempotent, consent changes take effect immediately, delivery remains auditable, and channels migrate incrementally with no lost messages.

Refactor the NestJS/MongoDB assessment store into a versioned PostgreSQL model with separate item banks, exams, attempts, responses, accommodations, and scoring snapshots. Preserve externally visible IDs, randomized delivery, time limits, offline sync, instructor review, and immutable submitted answers; use an expand-and-contract migration with dual reads and resumable backfill. The new schema must support institution-level retention and legal holds. Acceptance: old and new scoring agree on golden exams, concurrent submissions remain ordered, backfill checksums reconcile, recovery is tested, and cutover completes without taking active assessments offline.

Refactor the Java/Kotlin integration layer into a common adapter framework for LTI 1.3, OneRoster, Google Classroom, Canvas, and Microsoft Graph. Normalize identities, courses, memberships, assignments, and grades while preserving each provider's quirks behind tested adapters. Use OAuth2/OIDC, encrypted secrets, durable queues, rate-limit handling, idempotency keys, and dead-letter replay; existing district mappings must survive. Acceptance: current sync fixtures remain equivalent, duplicate webhooks are harmless, partial outages recover automatically, credentials rotate without downtime, and each connector can be versioned and deployed independently.

Refactor the multi-tenant Django/React platform so tenant isolation is enforced consistently at API, database, cache, object-storage, background-job, and analytics boundaries. Introduce typed authorization policies and PostgreSQL row-level security behind a compatibility layer, preserving existing roles and district-specific permissions. Audit every cross-tenant query, migrate legacy records safely, and keep operational support access explicitly scoped and logged. Acceptance: automated negative tests prove no tenant leakage, authorized workflows remain behaviorally compatible, performance stays within 10 percent of baseline, migrations are reversible, and security review signs off before enforcement is enabled.

Refactor the education search subsystem from Elasticsearch 6 to OpenSearch with an event-driven indexing pipeline shared by courses, lessons, users, and standards. Preserve analyzer behavior, synonyms, filters, ranking expectations, tenant ACLs, and zero-result telemetry while removing synchronous writes from request paths. Use TypeScript workers, Kafka offsets, versioned index templates, and blue/green aliases; support replay from canonical PostgreSQL data. Acceptance: relevance and permission regression suites pass, lag and recovery meet SLA, full reindex is repeatable, cutover is zero-downtime, and rollback restores the old index.

Refactor telemetry across the Go services and React clients into a canonical xAPI-compatible learning-event platform with a versioned envelope, ownership rules, and shared SDKs. Replace duplicate ad hoc payloads while preserving downstream research exports, intervention triggers, and institution-level reporting. Route events through Kafka into object storage and a queryable warehouse, with consent filtering, PII redaction, ordering metadata, deduplication, and replayable retention policies. Acceptance: all producers publish validated schemas, historical consumers remain compatible, event loss is measurable and below the current threshold, replays are idempotent, and migration coverage is visible in CI.

Refactor the React/TypeScript design system and server-rendered lesson UI into accessible primitives shared by the LMS, authoring tools, and assessment player. Target WCAG 2.2 AA, keyboard-only operation, screen-reader semantics, reduced motion, high contrast, localization expansion, and touch input without changing product workflows. Preserve component APIs through a staged compatibility layer and migrate hundreds of screens with visual regression coverage. Acceptance: axe and lint gates are clean, NVDA/VoiceOver smoke tests pass, no critical regressions remain at supported breakpoints, and teams can consume versioned packages independently.

Add one GitHub Actions workflow at `.github/workflows/extension-release.yml` for the existing Manifest V3 Chromium extension. On tags matching `v*`, run on Ubuntu with Node 20, `npm ci`, the existing test command, and the existing production build, then zip only `dist/` and attach the archive to a GitHub Release. Use least-privilege permissions, fail on any command error, and do not publish to a browser store. Acceptance: the tag workflow produces one reproducible extension zip and a release asset.

Fix the existing release workflow so its browser-extension archive contains only the distributable files from `dist/`, with `manifest.json` at the archive root. Exclude `node_modules`, repository metadata, test fixtures, and source maps, while preserving the current build and release commands. Keep the existing tag trigger and asset name unchanged. Acceptance: inspecting a generated zip shows the expected Manifest V3 files at root, no forbidden directories, and the GitHub Release upload still succeeds.

Add a validation step to the existing extension CI workflow after the production build. In one YAML file, inspect `dist/manifest.json` and fail the job unless it is Manifest V3, has nonempty `name` and `version` fields, declares a background service worker, and uses only the approved permissions `storage` and `activeTab`. Do not change application sources or the checked-in manifest. Acceptance: invalid build output fails with a readable message, while the current valid extension passes and continues to packaging.

Add a GitHub Actions job for the Firefox build that runs only on version tags, using Node 20 and the repository’s existing build command. Package the generated `dist/` directory as an XPI and sign it with `web-ext sign` using the `AMO_JWT_ISSUER` and `AMO_JWT_SECRET` GitHub secrets. Upload the signed XPI as the workflow artifact without printing credentials or publishing unrelated builds. Acceptance: a matching tag produces a signed XPI, missing secrets fail clearly, and pull requests do not invoke signing.

Update the existing GitHub Actions workflow for the Chromium extension to cache npm dependencies through `actions/setup-node` using the checked-in `package-lock.json`. Keep the current Node version, test command, build command, triggers, and artifact behavior unchanged. The cache key must vary when the lockfile changes and must not cache `dist/` or generated release archives. Acceptance: the first run saves a dependency cache, later runs report a cache hit, and a lockfile change creates a new cache entry.

Create or adjust one pull-request GitHub Actions workflow for the Manifest V3 browser extension. It should install dependencies with `npm ci`, run the existing tests and production build, zip `dist/`, and upload that zip as a workflow artifact for reviewers. It must never call Chrome Web Store or Firefox Add-ons publishing APIs, and artifact retention should be seven days. Acceptance: every non-draft pull request gets a downloadable preview archive, failures block the job, and no store credentials are required.

Repair the existing Firefox release workflow’s secret wiring in one YAML file. Pass the GitHub Actions secrets `AMO_JWT_ISSUER` and `AMO_JWT_SECRET` to `web-ext sign` through environment variables or supported flags, retaining the current tag trigger, build output, and XPI artifact name. Do not hard-code, echo, or expose either value in logs. Acceptance: the signing step receives both secrets under their documented names, a missing secret fails before upload, and the workflow remains unchanged for pull requests.

Extend the existing Chrome Web Store deployment workflow with a manual `workflow_dispatch` input named `release_tag`. When supplied, it must download the matching ZIP asset from the GitHub Release and send that archive to the existing store-upload command, bypassing the normal build. Keep automatic tag deployments unchanged, require only read access to release contents, and never delete or unpublish anything. Acceptance: an operator can select a prior tag and redeploy its exact archive, while invalid tags fail before upload with a clear error.

Extend the release workflow for the browser extension so that, after the production build, it uploads `dist/**/*.map` files to the existing Sentry project using `sentry-cli` and the `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` secret. Keep source maps out of the final release ZIP, preserve the current archive contents and asset name, and ensure the token is never logged. Acceptance: a valid release uploads maps before packaging, an upload failure fails the job, and the published archive contains no `.map` files.

Harden the existing Chrome Web Store upload step in one GitHub Actions workflow file. Keep its credentials, command, and archive path unchanged, but wrap the command in a maximum-three-attempt retry loop with a 30-second delay and set a ten-minute step timeout. Print only attempt status, fail the job after the final error, and avoid uploading again after a successful attempt. Acceptance: transient failures retry, a first-attempt success exits immediately, and persistent failures produce a nonzero workflow result.

Simplify the extension CI matrix in `.github/workflows/extension-ci.yml` so the existing test and build job runs only on Ubuntu with Node 20. Remove the obsolete Node 18 entry and any duplicate operating-system entries, but keep the current triggers, dependency installation, commands, and artifact naming. Do not change application code or release behavior. Acceptance: the workflow has one supported matrix combination, runs the same checks as before, and no longer reports failures from the unsupported Node version.

Adjust one release workflow file so the Manifest V3 service-worker entry is copied to `dist/background.js` before the extension is zipped, and verify that `dist/manifest.json` points to that path. Use the existing build output and do not alter application sources or the checked-in manifest. Add shell checks that both files exist and fail with a clear error before upload. Acceptance: the generated ZIP contains `manifest.json` and `background.js` at the expected paths, and the current release action receives the same artifact name.

Add request guardrails to the existing TypeScript/Express GitHub webhook bot. Update the Python Celery worker that processes bot jobs from Redis so transient failures retry automatically. Use exponential backoff with jitter, cap attempts at five, and route exhausted jobs to the existing dead-letter queue without retrying validation errors. Include the job ID and attempt number in structured logs, keep retries idempotent, and expose the retry count in the existing metrics. Add focused unit tests using a fake broker and document the new settings. Acceptance: one permanent failure creates one dead-letter record.

Create a GitHub Actions deployment workflow for the existing Dockerized Node.js GitHub App bot. On pushes to main, run lint and tests, build and tag the image, push it to GitHub Container Registry, and deploy the new digest to the existing AWS ECS Fargate service. Use OIDC with an assumed AWS role; do not add static cloud credentials. Pin action versions, add least-privilege permissions, and support manual rollback by image tag. Acceptance: pull requests remain test-only and a successful main run updates ECS.

Add a Kubernetes CronJob that prunes completed bot execution records older than 30 days from the PostgreSQL-backed automation service. Implement the deletion in the existing Python management command with a dry-run flag, batch deletes to avoid long locks, and emit a summary count. Configure the CronJob for 02:30 UTC, non-overlapping execution, a service account with only the required database secret, and failed-job retries. Add tests for the cutoff and dry-run behavior. Acceptance: applying the manifest creates one scheduled cleanup job and leaves active runs untouched.

Dockerize the existing Node.js notification bot as a production image. Add a multi-stage Dockerfile using the project’s locked package manager, run as a non-root user, and include only production dependencies and compiled output. Provide a /healthz check or equivalent process health probe, pass configuration through environment variables, and set a sensible stop signal. Update the local Compose file only if needed for parity. Acceptance: the image builds reproducibly, starts without source files, passes the health check, and does not contain secrets.

Wire AWS Secrets Manager rotation to an automatic rollout of the Kubernetes deployment running the automation bot. Add an EventBridge rule filtered to the target secret’s rotation completion event, invoke the existing TypeScript Lambda, and patch only the matching deployment to pick up the new version. Manage the rule, IAM permissions, and Lambda environment through Terraform; never log secret contents. Add tests for event filtering and deployment selection. Acceptance: a matching event triggers one rollout, unrelated secrets are ignored, and terraform plan is clean.

Configure KEDA autoscaling for the existing Kubernetes worker that consumes bot jobs from Redis. Replace the fixed replica count with a ScaledObject using the queue length trigger, minimum zero replicas, maximum ten, and a short cooldown suitable for bursty automation. Preserve the worker’s resource requests and add a polling/auth secret reference without embedding credentials. Include a staging overlay and validation notes. Acceptance: manifests apply successfully, an empty queue scales to zero, and a backlog increases replicas without changing the worker command.

Add Slack notifications for failed automation runs in the existing Python worker. Send one Block Kit message when a run reaches a terminal failure, including bot name, run ID, failure summary, environment, and a link to logs. Use the existing Slack incoming-webhook secret, make the channel configurable, and deduplicate retries so transient failures do not spam. Handle Slack errors without failing the worker, and add mocked unit tests. Acceptance: one terminal failure sends one message and the payload contains no tokens or raw secrets.

Use Terraform to provision a staging deployment for the existing Go automation bot on AWS ECS Fargate. Reuse the existing VPC and subnets, create a task definition with CPU and memory limits, pull the image from ECR, inject runtime secrets from Secrets Manager, and send container logs to a dedicated CloudWatch group. Add an ECS service with a health check, deployment circuit breaker, and outputs for service name and log group. Acceptance: terraform validate passes, the plan is limited to staging resources, and the task runs without plaintext secrets.

Create ephemeral preview environments for pull requests that change the bot’s automation code. Extend the GitHub Actions workflow to build the image, create a uniquely named Kubernetes namespace, deploy the chart with the PR image tag, and comment the preview URL on the PR. Add a cleanup job on PR close or cancellation, use concurrency to prevent stale updates, and grant only namespace-scoped permissions where possible. Acceptance: opening a PR creates one preview, updates replace the prior release, and closing it removes all preview resources.

Add an audit trail for actions performed by the existing TypeScript automation bot. Create a PostgreSQL migration and repository method that append an immutable record containing actor, trigger, bot, action, target, outcome, timestamp, and request ID. Write records for both successful and denied actions without blocking the main job when audit storage is temporarily unavailable; emit a structured warning instead. Add tests for field completeness and failure handling. Acceptance: every attempted privileged action produces one audit record and logs never include credentials.

Extend the existing TypeScript GitHub App and Slack integration with a production-release approval bot. When the release workflow requests approval, post a message with version, commit, environment, and an expiration time; accept approval only from an allowlisted maintainer through a verified Slack interaction, then approve the matching GitHub deployment. Reject duplicate, expired, or mismatched requests and record the decision. Add mocked API tests and document required secrets. Acceptance: one valid approval unblocks only its release, while unauthorized clicks do nothing.

Build a research-grade authentication security test platform for our Go microservices and React/TypeScript admin console. Cover OIDC, WebAuthn, refresh-token rotation, device binding, MFA recovery, session fixation, CSRF, brute force, tenant isolation, RBAC, and clock skew using PostgreSQL, Redis, and Kubernetes. Add property-based and fuzz tests, deterministic ephemeral environments, seeded attack fixtures, parallel CI shards, and signed reports. Acceptance: critical flows have branch-level coverage, OWASP abuse cases reproduce reliably, tests run locally and in GitHub Actions, failures include minimal reproducers, and no secrets leave the harness.

Create a distributed conformance and integration suite for SAML 2.0 and OIDC federation across our Kotlin/Spring identity service, Node.js gateway, and multi-tenant PostgreSQL deployment. Exercise metadata rotation, algorithm downgrade prevention, issuer confusion, audience checks, clock skew, logout propagation, SCIM deprovisioning, JIT provisioning, and identity-provider outages with real Okta, Azure AD, and mock providers. Use Testcontainers, WireMock, property-based generators, and Kubernetes fault injection. Acceptance: protocol vectors pass, cross-tenant access is impossible, retries are idempotent, compatibility reports are versioned, and CI blocks regressions.

Write an end-to-end security test program for the secrets delivery path spanning Python workers, a Go API, HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS, GitHub Actions, and Kubernetes. Test lease renewal, revocation, namespace isolation, rotation races, cached credentials, audit-log integrity, compromised runners, accidental log exposure, and disaster recovery. Build ephemeral Vault and KMS-compatible fixtures, fuzz policy inputs, scan generated artifacts, and run scheduled adversarial jobs. Acceptance: every secret has a tested lifecycle, leaked values are detected before release, tampering is observable, recovery meets the documented RTO/RPO, and CI publishes signed evidence.

Replace the legacy cryptography test collection with a Rust-based conformance and fuzzing system used by our C++ and Java services. Cover AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, Ed25519, X25519, key derivation, serialization, nonce misuse, invalid encodings, provider differences, and backward-compatible key rotation. Consume NIST and RFC vectors, add differential tests against OpenSSL and BoringSSL, run libFuzzer under sanitizers, and preserve reproducible seeds. Acceptance: all vectors pass on Linux and macOS, no secret material is logged, crashes become minimized fixtures, performance budgets are enforced, and the old suite can be retired safely.

Build a privacy and security regression platform for our Scala/Spark data lake, Python feature jobs, and dbt models on S3 and Snowflake. Test PII discovery, purpose-based access, row and column masking, deletion propagation, retention expiry, consent withdrawal, pseudonymization, lineage, and exports across batch and streaming paths. Generate synthetic but realistic identities, inject policy violations, and run isolated multi-tenant environments in Terraform-managed AWS accounts. Acceptance: every classified field has executable controls, deletion completes within the SLA, unauthorized joins fail, audit evidence is immutable, and tests gate merges and nightly production-like runs.

Create a research-grade payment-boundary test suite for Java/Kotlin services using Kafka, PostgreSQL, Redis, and Stripe plus bank-adapter sandboxes. Cover idempotency, replayed webhooks, authorization gaps, double capture, partial refunds, ledger invariants, PCI redaction, tenant isolation, key rotation, timeout recovery, and out-of-order events. Build contract tests, model-based state-machine tests, fault injection, and deterministic replay of production-shaped traces without real customer data. Acceptance: ledger balances never drift, duplicate money movement is impossible, every security invariant has a failing test, and CI produces auditable evidence.

Implement a continuous security-exercise harness for our Kubernetes platform, including Go services, Envoy, ArgoCD, and an OpenTelemetry pipeline. Automate adversarial drills for stolen service-account tokens, lateral movement, supply-chain image tampering, network-policy bypass, log forgery, and degraded observability, using isolated clusters and synthetic identities. Add chaos scheduling, rollback controls, evidence capture, and severity scoring without touching production data. Acceptance: each scenario has a deterministic oracle, blast radius is bounded, alerts and runbooks are validated end to end, results are signed, and failed controls open actionable regressions.

Migrate the security regression harness from our Perl/Jenkins monolith to a Python/pytest platform running in GitHub Actions and ephemeral Kubernetes namespaces. Preserve and expand coverage for TLS policy, SSO, authorization, dependency provenance, container scanning, and destructive API misuse while eliminating order dependence and flaky timing assumptions. Add shared fixtures, parallel sharding, historical trend storage, migration adapters, and reproducible local execution. Acceptance: old and new suites agree during a dual-run period, no critical test is lost, runtime is cut by half, findings retain ownership and severity, and the Jenkins jobs can be decommissioned.

Design an authorization oracle and property-based test system for a multi-tenant TypeScript/Node.js platform with PostgreSQL row-level security and an OPA/Rego policy service. Model RBAC, ABAC, delegated administration, resource inheritance, time-bounded grants, revocation, and cross-tenant aliases; compare API decisions with database enforcement under concurrency. Include mutation testing, generated policy graphs, differential evaluation across OPA versions, and a corpus of historical incidents. Acceptance: every deny/allow decision is explainable, privilege-escalation mutations fail, race conditions are reproducible, policies are backward-compatible unless approved, and CI blocks unexplained authorization drift.

Build a disaster-recovery test system for encrypted backups of our Go/PostgreSQL service across AWS us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Exercise envelope-key rotation, KMS outage, credential loss, corrupted snapshots, partial restores, point-in-time recovery, tenant-selective restore, compromised operators, and region failover. Use Terraform, LocalStack where valid, real staging KMS keys, and synthetic datasets with checksums and PII controls. Acceptance: documented RTO/RPO are proven quarterly, restored data passes integrity and authorization checks, no plaintext artifacts persist, failover is repeatable, and signed evidence is retained for audits.

Create a security test and fuzzing program for a Rust plugin runtime embedded in our desktop Electron/TypeScript application. Validate capability grants, process isolation, IPC authentication, filesystem and network escapes, malicious manifests, resource exhaustion, update rollback, signature verification, and downgrade resistance across macOS, Windows, and Linux. Build a corpus-driven fuzzer, sandbox escape probes, golden compatibility fixtures, crash minimization, and CI workers with least privilege. Acceptance: plugins cannot exceed declared capabilities, every escape attempt is contained and reported, signed updates reject tampering, crashes produce reproducers, and release gates consume the results.

Develop a distributed security test platform for untrusted document uploads to our Python/FastAPI and Go processing pipeline. Cover polyglots, decompression bombs, malformed PDFs and Office files, macro and script detection, archive traversal, parser differentials, malware verdict races, quarantine bypasses, and tenant data leakage. Orchestrate ClamAV, sandbox detonation, object storage, Kafka, and PostgreSQL in disposable Kubernetes environments; never use live malware or customer files. Acceptance: unsafe content cannot reach downstream consumers, verdicts are idempotent and auditable, limits hold under load, every bypass becomes a regression fixture, and CI provides signed reports.

Support automated health checks, database migration gates, traffic switching, approval checkpoints for production, fast rollback, and cleanup of the inactive environment. Preserve stable service discovery and session behavior while deployments run. Acceptance requires staging demonstrations, failure-injection tests, versioned rollout configuration, deployment metrics and alerts, documented operator procedures, and a rollback completing within five minutes without dropped requests.

Build reusable Terraform modules for the AWS platform, including VPC networking, EKS, RDS, IAM, KMS, S3, DNS, and observability integrations. Support isolated dev, staging, and production environments with shared conventions, remote state, secure provider configuration, and explicit dependency boundaries. Add GitHub Actions plan/apply workflows, OPA or Conftest policy checks, drift detection, import guidance, and documented upgrade procedures. Acceptance requires reproducible environment creation, reviewed plans, least-privilege IAM, encrypted state and data, destroy-safe defaults, and a migration path from existing manually managed resources.

Create an incident-response subsystem integrating PagerDuty, Slack, and a small Go service backed by PostgreSQL. It must normalize alerts, deduplicate repeated events, open and update incidents idempotently, manage escalation and acknowledgement state, record an immutable audit trail, and publish status updates.
