Acceptance requires contract and integration tests, replayable event fixtures, dashboards for alert delivery latency and failures, runbooks for degraded dependencies, and a staged deployment that preserves existing PagerDuty behavior.

Rework Kubernetes capacity management using HPA, KEDA, Prometheus Adapter, Cluster Autoscaler, and topology-aware scheduling. Establish scaling policies for CPU, memory, queue depth, and request latency; remove conflicting or ineffective rules; and align resource requests, limits, PodDisruptionBudgets, and startup probes with actual workload behavior. Cover node groups, spot capacity, graceful draining, and maximum-cost safeguards. Acceptance requires production-like load tests, documented SLO and cost tradeoffs, predictable scale-up and scale-down behavior, alerting for unschedulable pods, and rollback-tested Helm configuration.

Design and implement disaster recovery for PostgreSQL, Redis, object storage, and Kubernetes workloads across two AWS regions. Use encrypted backups, PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery, cross-region S3 replication, Redis recovery procedures, and Velero for cluster resources. Define an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of one hour, including DNS, secrets, dependencies, and application configuration. Acceptance requires automated backup verification, isolated-account restore tests, quarterly game-day scripts, checksum and consistency checks, failure alerts, access controls, and operator documentation proving the targets are achievable.

Harden the EKS platform against common workload and supply-chain risks using Pod Security Admission, Kyverno, NetworkPolicy, strict RBAC, IRSA, private endpoints, and Cosign image-signature verification. Inventory current exceptions, separate enforcement by environment, and provide a controlled process for temporary waivers with expiry and ownership. Update base images, admission policies, CI checks, and operational documentation. Acceptance requires policy unit tests, a CIS-aligned assessment, successful deployment of existing services, blocked negative test cases, actionable audit logs, and a tested emergency rollback path.

Create an internal deployment platform built around GitHub Actions, Argo CD, Helm, and Backstage. Provide a golden path for registering services, creating repositories, configuring environments, promoting releases, managing approvals, injecting secrets, and rolling back safely. Standardize ownership metadata, health checks, deployment history, audit events, and operational links while allowing controlled customization for exceptional workloads. Acceptance requires templates for at least two representative services, dev-to-production promotion, policy enforcement, failure recovery, onboarding documentation, and evidence that a new service can deploy without hand-written platform changes.

Implement multi-region failover for Aurora PostgreSQL Global Database with RDS Proxy, Route 53 health checks, application retry policies, and a controlled promotion workflow. Define behavior for writer loss, region isolation, stale reads, connection draining, schema migrations, and operator-initiated failback; prevent split brain and accidental writes to the old primary. Acceptance requires an automated health and readiness model, encrypted replication, observability for lag and promotion state, a game-day runbook, failure-injection tests, and measured failover under five minutes with an RPO below one minute.

Operationalize a production Kafka platform on EKS using Strimzi, with TLS and SCRAM authentication, ACLs, quotas, schema governance, and tiered topic policies. Provide multi-AZ brokers, persistent storage, partition and retention standards, MirrorMaker 2 replication to a secondary region, Prometheus monitoring, and safe rolling upgrades. Define producer and consumer failure behavior, dead-letter handling, and ownership metadata. Acceptance requires load and rebalance tests, simulated broker and region failures, lag and disk alerts, documented capacity planning, backup or recovery procedures, and an upgrade rehearsal without data loss.

Add FinOps guardrails across AWS and Kubernetes using Cost and Usage Reports, OpenCost, tagging policies, budgets, and automated notifications. Attribute spend to teams, services, environments, and shared infrastructure; identify idle resources and oversized workloads; and expose daily and monthly trends in Grafana. Add policy checks for missing tags, budget thresholds, unowned resources, and risky provisioning, while keeping an approval path for exceptions. Acceptance requires reconciled billing data, actionable Slack or email alerts, rightsizing recommendations, documented ownership, and a pilot covering production workloads.

In the existing TypeScript Chrome Manifest V3 extension, add an options-page usage analytics view backed by the extension’s local event store. Aggregate daily counts for popup opens, content-script actions, and completed tasks over selectable 7, 30, and 90-day ranges; exclude raw URLs and user text. Add a lightweight table, sparkline-style CSS bars, and loading and empty states. Acceptance: aggregates match fixture data, date filters update without reload, sensitive fields never render, and unit tests cover timezone boundaries and no-event cases.

Add a CSV export action to the existing TypeScript Chrome Manifest V3 analytics page. Export the currently filtered event aggregates, not raw browsing content, with columns for date, event name, count, and unique installation count. Respect the selected date range and event filters, escape commas, quotes, and newlines, and use a deterministic UTF-8 filename. Keep generation in the extension UI without a server dependency. Acceptance: downloaded CSV opens correctly in spreadsheet software, zero-row exports contain headers, filters are honored, and tests cover escaping and filename dates.

Implement a conversion-funnel report in the extension’s React options page using the existing local event store. Define ordered steps as extension install, first popup open, first content action, and completed task; show users reaching each step, step-to-step conversion percentages, and overall conversion. Handle repeated events and missing steps without inflating counts, and do not change the stored event schema. Acceptance: fixture-driven tests verify ordering and deduplication, an empty dataset renders a useful state, percentages are stable, and the report works across the supported date filters.

Create a click-heatmap summary for the browser extension’s content-script interactions. In the TypeScript analytics view, group existing interaction events by normalized target label and show the top targets with counts and percentage of total clicks; never display page text, query strings, or full URLs. Add a simple CSS intensity scale and a date-range selector rather than rendering a screenshot. Acceptance: labels are normalized consistently, unknown targets fall into an “Other” bucket, fixture totals reconcile with raw event counts, empty data is handled, and unit tests cover URL redaction and sorting ties.

Add weekly cohort-retention analysis to the extension’s analytics view. Define each cohort by the first recorded active date for an installation, then calculate week 0 through week 4 returning-active percentages from the existing local event records. Use calendar weeks consistently in the extension’s configured timezone, exclude incomplete future weeks, and keep installation identifiers inside aggregation logic. Acceptance: the table shows cohort size and retention percentages, small cohorts do not produce divide-by-zero errors, fixture results are deterministic, and tests cover users active across week boundaries.

Add a latency breakdown panel to the browser extension’s diagnostics page using existing timing events from the service worker and content scripts. Report request, parsing, rendering, and total durations with count, median, p95, and maximum for the selected date range. Ignore malformed or negative durations and clearly indicate when a segment has no samples. Do not add a remote telemetry service. Acceptance: calculations match hand-checked fixtures, percentile behavior is documented and tested, the panel remains responsive for 10,000 events, and the TypeScript build and unit suite pass.

Fix duplicate event counts in the extension’s local analytics aggregation. The TypeScript query layer should treat records with the same event ID as one event, while preserving distinct events that share a timestamp or name; legacy records without IDs should use the existing timestamp-and-payload fallback key. Do not delete stored records or alter ingestion behavior. Acceptance: daily totals and unique-user counts are corrected, repeated reads remain stable, events from different days are not merged, and regression tests cover mixed legacy and modern records.

Add a privacy metrics section to the browser extension’s options dashboard. Analyze existing consent, consent-withdrawal, and telemetry-disabled events by day, showing opt-in rate, withdrawal rate, and the number of installations with no decision. Use only aggregated local data, exclude identifiers and page content, and make the denominator explicit when no consent event exists. Acceptance: metrics reconcile against fixture timelines, withdrawals are counted once per installation per state change, the UI explains the definitions, and tests cover missing consent records and date-range filtering.

Build a local search-insights table for the extension’s own search feature. From existing search events, show total searches, zero-result rate, and the ten most frequent normalized terms for the selected period. Trim whitespace, compare case-insensitively, and exclude empty queries; do not send terms to a server or expose them in logs. Acceptance: repeated searches are counted correctly, zero-result calculations use only completed searches, ties sort deterministically, the table has loading and empty states, and unit tests verify normalization, filtering, and date boundaries.

Add a weekly trend-alert summary to the extension’s analytics page. Compare each tracked event’s latest complete week with the preceding week and flag increases or decreases beyond a configurable percentage threshold, requiring at least ten events in both periods. Show the metric, prior value, current value, and direction; avoid browser notifications or network calls. Acceptance: thresholds are validated, incomplete weeks are excluded, insufficient samples produce no alert, results sort by absolute change, and fixture-based tests cover zero baselines and exact-threshold behavior.

Add a referrer-domain report to the extension’s local analytics view. Parse the existing navigation events with the standard URL API, discard invalid values, reduce each referrer to its hostname, and show counts and share of total for the selected period. Exclude paths, query parameters, fragments, and private browsing URLs from the rendered output. Acceptance: subdomains follow the repository’s documented grouping rule, totals reconcile with valid events, sorting is deterministic, no raw URL is displayed, and tests cover malformed URLs, missing referrers, and date filtering.

Add a lightweight anomaly panel to the Chrome extension’s analytics page for daily event counts. For each tracked event, calculate a rolling seven-day mean and standard deviation, flag days whose count exceeds two standard deviations from the baseline, and require at least five baseline days. Keep the computation local and deterministic; do not introduce machine-learning dependencies. Acceptance: flagged dates and scores match fixed fixtures, zero-variance baselines do not create false positives, incomplete current days are excluded, the UI explains the rule, and unit tests cover sparse data and boundary values.

Build a production-grade zero-trust service-to-service platform for 20+ Kubernetes clusters on AWS EKS using Istio, SPIFFE/SPIRE, Terraform, and Helm. Replace static network trust with workload identity, mTLS, authorization policies, and egress controls, while preserving gradual namespace-by-namespace rollout. Add highly available control planes, multi-account federation, certificate rotation, policy testing, audit export to S3/OpenSearch, and break-glass access. Acceptance: reproducible staging and production plans, no plaintext service traffic, automated conformance tests, documented rollback, and demonstrated regional control-plane failure recovery.

Move application and CI secrets from scattered Kubernetes Secrets, GitHub Actions variables, and AWS SSM into a highly available HashiCorp Vault cluster on AWS, provisioned with Terraform and deployed via Helm. Define namespaces, authentication methods, least-privilege policies, dynamic database and cloud credentials, automatic rotation, replication, backup and restore, and migration tooling that avoids downtime. Acceptance: complete inventory coverage, zero leaked values in Git or logs, dual-read cutover with rollback, disaster-recovery drill, audited access, and runbooks for operators and developers.

Create a multi-cluster Kubernetes security admission platform using Gatekeeper/OPA, Kyverno where appropriate, and policy bundles distributed through Argo CD. Cover privileged containers, host mounts, image provenance, resource limits, network policy, namespace tenancy, and Pod Security Standards, with warn-to-enforce rollout and explicit emergency exemptions. Include Rego tests, signed versioned bundles, policy observability, developer feedback, and upgrade compatibility for EKS and GKE. Acceptance: policy decisions are auditable, bypasses expire automatically, CI blocks violations, and all clusters converge from Git.

Design and implement a secure multi-region disaster-recovery platform for an AWS-hosted Kubernetes estate spanning EKS, RDS PostgreSQL, S3, and Terraform state. Use separate accounts, KMS keys, private connectivity, immutable backups, and least-privilege recovery roles; automate regional failover with Argo CD and AWS Backup while preventing split brain and credential reuse. Define RPO/RTO tiers, dependency ordering, DNS cutover, evidence capture, and rollback. Acceptance: quarterly game-day automation restores representative services, meets documented RPO/RTO, passes access audits, and leaves no untracked infrastructure.

Implement an end-to-end software supply-chain security system for containerized Go and Python services. Add reproducible builds in GitHub Actions, SBOM generation with Syft, vulnerability policy with Grype, artifact signing and provenance attestations with Sigstore Cosign and SLSA, and admission verification in Kubernetes. Mirror approved dependencies and images into an AWS ECR-based promotion path with quarantine and expiry. Acceptance: unsigned or unprovenanced workloads cannot deploy, exceptions are time-bound and audited, releases are traceable to commits, and recovery from a compromised builder is documented and tested.

Build a security incident-response platform integrating Kubernetes audit logs, AWS CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Okta, GitHub, and PagerDuty. Use Kafka or Kinesis for durable ingestion, a normalized event schema, rule-based detection, enrichment, case management, and immutable evidence retention in S3/OpenSearch. Support tenant isolation, RBAC, deduplication, replay, alert suppression, and on-call escalation without exposing secrets. Acceptance: replayable fixtures produce known detections, ingestion survives regional outages, detection latency and retention SLOs are measured, and responders can export a complete chain of custody.

Lead a large migration from long-lived AWS IAM users and shared access keys to centralized workforce and workload identity using Okta, AWS IAM Identity Center, OIDC, and GitHub Actions federation. Inventory permissions across multiple AWS organizations, map roles to teams, apply permission boundaries and SCPs, and stage revocation with break-glass controls. Provide Terraform modules, access reviews, telemetry, and automated key retirement. Acceptance: no unmanaged human keys remain, CI uses short-lived credentials, least-privilege tests pass, service owners sign off, and rollback is rehearsed.

Create an organization-wide secrets rotation service for PostgreSQL, Redis, SaaS APIs, TLS certificates, and cloud credentials across Kubernetes and VM workloads. Implement a Go controller and event-driven workers using Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, cert-manager, and Argo Workflows, with dependency-aware rollout, dual credentials, revocation, retries, and audit records. Support hundreds of services without synchronized outages and provide dry-run previews. Acceptance: rotations complete within declared SLOs, consumers reload safely, failed rotations self-heal or page operators, old values are revoked, and chaos tests demonstrate recovery.

Develop a centralized policy-as-code platform for infrastructure security using Open Policy Agent, Rego, Terraform plan scanning, Kubernetes admission, and a versioned policy registry. Provide reusable controls for encryption, public exposure, logging, IAM, data residency, and approved regions, with ownership metadata and exception workflows. Run policies consistently in pull requests, CI, deployment gates, and periodic drift scans; publish signed decision evidence to a compliance store. Acceptance: policy results are deterministic across environments, exceptions expire, false positives are measurable, and auditors can trace every deployed resource to a decision.

Replace bespoke VPN and bastion access with a federated, identity-aware access plane for engineers and vendors reaching private AWS, Kubernetes, databases, and internal admin tools. Use WireGuard or Cloudflare Zero Trust for network access, Okta device posture and MFA, short-lived SSH and database credentials, session recording, and just-in-time approvals. Model tenants and environments separately, preserve emergency access, and migrate users in waves. Acceptance: no shared bastion accounts remain, access is policy-driven and logged, revocation takes minutes, vendor scope is bounded, and failover plus audit exports are tested.

Build a secure software distribution and update pipeline for air-gapped Kubernetes environments. In the connected zone, scan and sign container images, Helm charts, OS packages, and SBOMs; transfer approved bundles through an encrypted, malware-scanned artifact exchange; then verify signatures and provenance offline before promotion. Support multiple disconnected sites, monotonic versioning, rollback, key rotation, revocation manifests, and operator approval. Acceptance: no unapproved artifact can install, transfers are tamper-evident, sites can recover from failed updates, and end-to-end evidence satisfies offline audit requirements.

Create a governed security telemetry platform that collects high-volume logs and traces from Kubernetes, cloud accounts, hosts, identity providers, and CI/CD. Use OpenTelemetry collectors, Kafka, ClickHouse or OpenSearch, and object storage with tenant-aware RBAC and immutable retention tiers. Define redaction and data-minimization rules, schema evolution, clock handling, sampling, detection feeds, and disaster recovery. Acceptance: ingestion scales through peak load, sensitive fields are demonstrably removed, queries meet analyst latency targets, retention and deletion policies are enforced, and replayed incidents reproduce expected timelines.

In the existing Python/pandas analytics module, implement only `summarize_attendance_outliers` in `attendance.py`. It should accept rows with `course_id`, `student_id`, `status`, and `date`, exclude `excused` absences, calculate each course’s absence rate over the requested date range, and flag courses at least 10 percentage points above the median course rate. Return deterministic records containing `course_id`, `absence_rate`, and `student_count`, sorted by rate descending then ID. Empty input returns an empty list; do not change database schemas or UI. Existing analytics tests must continue passing.

Within the TypeScript grade analytics file, add `buildGradeTrend(rows)` without changing API routes. Each row has `studentId`, `term`, and numeric `score`; group by term, report count, mean, and population standard deviation, and order terms using the repository’s existing term comparator. Ignore rows with missing or non-numeric scores. The function must return an empty array for no valid rows and preserve full precision in the object values. Add or update the focused unit fixture only if the file already contains tests; acceptance is a stable result for repeated input and passing existing test commands.

Implement `cohortCompletionSummary` in the existing Python service, using the current enrollment dictionaries rather than a new query. For each cohort, count enrolled learners and learners whose `completed_at` is non-null, then compute completion rate as completed divided by enrolled; cohorts with zero enrollment must report 0 rather than NaN. Return rows sorted by cohort start date, with `cohort_id`, `enrolled`, `completed`, and `completion_rate`. Preserve timezone-aware dates and ignore unrelated fields. This is a single-function change: no schema, endpoint, or dashboard work. Acceptance covers expected fixture values and empty input behavior.

In `quiz_metrics.ts`, implement one pure TypeScript function, `analyzeQuizItems(attempts)`, for attempts containing `quizId`, `itemId`, `correct`, and `answered`. Group by item, compute attempts, answer rate, and difficulty as correct answered attempts divided by answered attempts, and mark `needsReview` when difficulty is below 0.30 or above 0.90. Exclude unrecognized boolean values, avoid division by zero, and sort by `itemId`. Keep the existing exported types and do not touch storage or UI. Acceptance requires exact handling of unanswered attempts and an empty-result case.

Add `summarizeReadingGaps` to the existing Python/pandas reporting file. It receives rows with `grade`, `subgroup`, and `scaled_score`, computes each subgroup’s mean within each grade, and reports the difference from that grade’s overall mean. Suppress any subgroup with fewer than 10 valid scores and ignore missing scores. Return a stable list ordered by numeric grade then subgroup, with `grade`, `subgroup`, `n`, `mean`, and `gap`. Use the project’s existing rounding convention of two decimals, make no chart changes, and keep the calculation in one function. Acceptance covers small-group suppression, missing data, and empty input.

Update the existing TypeScript analytics exporter with one function, `kpisToCsv(kpis)`, for the school administrator KPI table. Emit the fixed header order `school_id,active_students,attendance_rate,completion_rate`, one newline-terminated row per KPI, and no extra columns. Escape commas, quotes, and line breaks using standard CSV quoting; render null or undefined as an empty field and percentages as the supplied numeric values without multiplying by 100. Preserve input order and return the header plus newline for an empty list. No package additions or UI changes; existing export tests must pass.

Implement `weeklyRetention` in the current Python analytics module. Given enrollment rows containing `student_id`, `course_id`, and `enrolled_at`, plus activity rows containing the same IDs and `occurred_at`, calculate unique active-student retention for weeks 0 through 8 relative to each student’s enrollment date. The denominator is the enrolled student count per course; missing activity yields zero retention, and duplicate events count once. Return deterministic course records with week arrays and rates rounded to four decimals. Keep it in one function, use existing date utilities, and leave database queries untouched.

In the existing survey reporting file, add a pure function `rollupSurveyResponses(responses)` for course feedback. Responses contain `courseId`, `questionId`, `rating` from 1–5, and optional `comment`; ignore invalid ratings and never return comment text. Group by course and question, returning response count, mean rating, and the percentage of ratings at least 4. Sort by course ID then question ID, with means and percentages rounded to two decimals. Empty or wholly invalid input returns `[]`. Do not alter the survey schema or frontend; acceptance is deterministic output for duplicate and missing-field cases.

Create `teacherWorkloadByWeek` in the existing Python education analytics file. It accepts assignment events with `teacher_id`, `course_id`, `week_start`, and `minutes_spent`; discard negative or non-numeric minutes, aggregate total minutes and assignment count per teacher per week, and calculate each teacher’s share of the weekly total. Return ISO-date-sorted rows with `teacher_id`, `week_start`, `assignment_count`, `minutes`, and `share`, using zero share when the weekly total is zero. Keep the calculation pure and limited to one function; no persistence or reporting-page changes. Existing fixtures must remain compatible.

Implement `assignBenchmarkBands` in the current TypeScript assessment module. Each score record has `studentId`, `grade`, and numeric `score` from 0 to 100. Assign `below`, `approaching`, `proficient`, or `advanced` using inclusive cutoffs of 0–59, 60–74, 75–89, and 90–100, preserving the input record plus a `band` field. Ignore records with missing, non-numeric, or out-of-range scores, and return results in original order. Keep the function pure and exported from the existing file; no UI changes. Acceptance includes boundary values, invalid rows, and an empty array.

Add `compareInterventionImpact` to the existing Python analytics module for a tutoring pilot. Input rows contain `student_id`, `group`, `pre_score`, and `post_score`. Exclude rows missing either score or having another group, compute each row’s change, then return group counts, mean change, and the intervention-minus-control difference in mean change. Round reported values to two decimals and return zero difference when one group has no valid rows. Treat every valid input row as one measurement; do not deduplicate students. Do not add statistical dependencies or modify storage. Focused tests must cover missing scores, duplicate students, and empty input.

Implement `buildCourseActivityDigest` in the existing Node.js analytics file. It receives activity rows with `courseId`, `day`, `studentId`, `eventType`, and optional `durationMinutes`; for each course, count unique active students, total events, submissions, and summed non-negative duration over the supplied seven-day window. Return courses sorted by `courseId`, omit courses with no valid events, and treat missing duration as zero. Keep event-type matching case-sensitive and avoid changing the database query. One function only; acceptance checks duplicate students, invalid durations, stable ordering, and empty input.

Implement an end-to-end, column-level lineage subsystem for dbt models in Snowflake. Parse dbt manifest and catalog artifacts plus SQL dependencies, persist a versioned graph in PostgreSQL, and expose authenticated REST endpoints and a CLI for upstream/downstream impact analysis. Support renamed columns, ephemeral models, cycles, stale manifests, and incremental refreshes. Acceptance requires deterministic graphs, migrations, fixtures, API contract tests, documented recovery, and impact queries under 500 ms for a 10,000-node graph.

Refactor the cohort-analysis service backed by PostgreSQL and Redis so recurring retention queries stop scanning raw events. Design partitioned fact tables, rollup and materialized-view refreshes, parameterized query plans, and cache invalidation for daily and monthly cohorts. Preserve existing API semantics and timezone rules, with a dual-read comparison period. Acceptance is identical results on a supplied corpus, p95 API latency below 2 seconds at 50 concurrent requests, explain-plan benchmarks, online migration scripts, load tests, and runbook coverage.

Replace the ad hoc metrics layer with a governed semantic model using dbt, BigQuery, and a small Python service. Define metric YAML for grain, dimensions, filters, owners, and certified SQL; generate reusable queries for dashboards and exports; prevent fanout joins and conflicting definitions. Support backward-compatible metric aliases and versioned changes. Acceptance includes at least 20 migrated metrics, compile-time validation, golden-result tests, lineage links, permission checks, documentation, and measured query-cost limits on representative workloads.

Design and implement event-retention management for the PostgreSQL analytics store fed by Kafka. Add time-based partitions, archival to S3 Parquet, configurable tenant policies, legal holds, and verifiable deletion of raw and derived records. Provide an operator API, scheduled workers, dry-run reports, retries, and audit logs without blocking ingestion. Acceptance requires idempotent jobs, referential-integrity handling, encrypted archives, recovery drills, migration tooling, metrics and alerts, and tests proving records disappear within the configured service-level window.

Build a production anomaly-detection pipeline for daily warehouse KPIs in Snowflake, orchestrated by Airflow and implemented in Python. Ingest metric definitions and historical series, calculate seasonality-aware baselines, detect missing data and statistical outliers, and store explainable findings for analysts. Include suppression, acknowledgement, and backfill workflows plus a queryable results API. Acceptance requires deterministic replay, tenant isolation, configurable thresholds, alert deduplication, late-arriving data handling, dashboard-ready tables, monitoring, and tests over seeded anomalous datasets.

Unify customer dimensions across PostgreSQL orders, SaaS billing, and Snowflake product usage using dbt and Python identity-resolution jobs. Establish canonical keys, deterministic and probabilistic match rules, survivorship precedence, and slowly changing dimension type 2 history without rewriting trusted facts. Produce exception queues and merge or unmerge audit trails for manual review. Acceptance includes reproducible mappings, privacy-safe handling of identifiers, incremental processing, reconciliation totals, downstream model updates, migration documentation, and tests for collisions, late updates, and reversals.

Migrate the largest PostgreSQL analytics tables to a partitioned design keyed by event date and tenant while keeping production reads and writes available. Profile query patterns, choose partition and index strategy, create online backfill and cutover tooling, and update ORM queries, retention jobs, and reporting views. The migration must support pause, resume, and rollback with bounded lock time. Acceptance requires no data loss, verified row-count and checksum parity, improved benchmark plans, deployment sequencing, operational metrics, and a documented rollback rehearsal.

Create an idempotent historical-aggregate backfill framework for ClickHouse tables used by reporting. It should accept a metric, time range, and versioned transformation, discover dependencies, schedule bounded parallel work, checkpoint progress, and write results atomically without corrupting current partitions. Include dry runs, sampling comparisons, retries, cancellation, and audit records visible to operators. Acceptance requires restart safety, reproducible outputs, resource limits, late-data handling, CLI and API controls, integration tests on a production-sized fixture, and an operator runbook.

Build a data-quality subsystem for dbt models in BigQuery, combining schema, freshness, uniqueness, referential, and business-rule checks. Store run results and historical distributions in PostgreSQL, classify failures by severity, quarantine unsafe partitions, and expose ownership, suppression, and acknowledgement workflows to analysts. Integrate with Airflow retries and deployment gates while preserving partial availability for unaffected models. Acceptance requires configurable thresholds, alert deduplication, lineage-aware impact lists, CI tests, seeded failure fixtures, dashboards, and documented escalation procedures.

Implement query-regression analysis for a PostgreSQL analytics cluster using pg_stat_statements, captured execution plans, and a Python ingestion service. Normalize queries, maintain per-fingerprint baselines, detect changes in latency, rows, buffers, and plan shape, and correlate regressions with deployments and schema migrations. Provide retention controls, an authenticated API, and actionable comparisons for engineers. Acceptance requires low-overhead collection, deterministic detection on replayed workloads, explain-plan storage limits, alert routing, index recommendations with evidence, tests, and an operations guide.

Build a governed reporting-snapshot export subsystem from Snowflake to S3 as partitioned Parquet. Support scheduled and on-demand runs, schema-versioned manifests, row-level PII masking, consistent point-in-time reads, encryption, signed delivery metadata, and resumable multipart uploads. Track lineage and consumer acknowledgements in PostgreSQL, with retention and revocation controls. Acceptance requires idempotent reruns, atomic publish semantics, schema compatibility checks, least-privilege roles, failure recovery, representative volume benchmarks, contract tests, and a documented consumer migration path.

Create a finance reconciliation service comparing PostgreSQL ledger facts with BigQuery sales and payment aggregates. Define a versioned reconciliation contract for time zones, currencies, fees, refunds, and settlement timing; load source snapshots, match at transaction and daily levels, classify tolerances, and persist immutable discrepancy cases. Provide reruns, evidence attachments, approvals, and exportable audit reports. Acceptance requires balanced control totals, deterministic results, late-arriving correction handling, access controls, performance on a year of data, integration tests, and an operator runbook.

In the Python repository, rename the root-level file `model.py` to `model_old.py` using a normal filesystem rename. Do not edit contents or touch other files. Acceptance: `model.py` is absent and `model_old.py` exists with identical contents.

In root-level `requirements.txt`, replace the existing NumPy requirement with exactly `numpy==1.26.4`. Preserve all other dependencies and their ordering. Acceptance: one line reads `numpy==1.26.4`, with no other NumPy version constraint in that file.

From the repository root, run exactly `git status --short` and return the command's output. Do not stage, modify, or delete anything. Acceptance: the response contains the current short status, including any modified or untracked files visible to Git.

Build a research-grade analytical workbench for the existing Electron/TypeScript desktop app. Add a Python service layer, DuckDB/Apache Arrow execution, versioned projects, parameterized pipelines, provenance, cached results, and reproducible export to Parquet, CSV, and HTML. Long-running jobs must survive restarts, use worker processes, and expose progress/cancellation. Keep sensitive datasets local by default, support optional S3-compatible storage, and preserve current plugins. Acceptance: deterministic reruns, 10-million-row demo workflow under documented limits, migration tooling, signed installers, unit/integration tests, and user documentation.

Extend the Electron/React desktop app into a telemetry exploration platform for billions of timestamped events. Implement an Arrow/Parquet ingestion pipeline, schema evolution, partition pruning, DuckDB local queries, and a remote Spark-compatible execution path with resumable jobs. Provide interactive time-series plots, faceting, filters, saved investigations, and shareable query specifications without uploading data unless enabled. Create an offline-first analytics workspace in the Tauri/Rust desktop client, backed by SQLite metadata and DuckDB analytical storage. Acceptance: production responses contain the headers and the app still loads and authenticates normally.

In the existing Chrome Manifest V3 extension, update the filtering function in `src/content/filter.ts` so it hides only elements matching the user’s configured CSS selectors. It must skip editable controls, iframes, and nodes already hidden by the page, while preserving selector order and case sensitivity. Return the number of newly hidden elements so the service worker can update the badge. Do not add dependencies or change storage. Acceptance: current tests pass, matching nodes are hidden once, skipped nodes are unchanged, and the returned count is accurate.

Add Enable/Disable behavior to the existing Manifest V3 extension popup using the already-present `#enabled-toggle` checkbox and only editing `src/popup.ts`. Use the existing `chrome.storage.sync` key `enabled`, defaulting to true when absent. Persist changes immediately and send the existing runtime message so content scripts apply the new state without a page reload. Preserve current popup styling and layout. Acceptance: opening the popup reflects stored state, toggling updates storage and message payload, and a disabled setting prevents the extension’s page action.

In the existing Manifest V3 service worker, fix the badge-update function so it displays the filtered-item count for the sender tab. Counts from the current tab must replace, not accumulate with, the previous value; zero should clear the badge, and values above 99 should display `99+`. Keep the existing `chrome.action` API and do not alter message names or storage. Acceptance: repeated updates show the latest count, tab IDs remain isolated, zero removes stale text, and the function handles a missing or nonnumeric count without throwing.

Add a Save page command to the extension’s service worker using the existing `chrome.contextMenus` setup. When invoked for the active tab, store its URL, title, and favicon in the existing `chrome.storage.local` array named `savedPages`. Ignore duplicate URLs, keep newest entries first, and cap the array at 50 items by dropping the oldest. Do not request new permissions or change the saved object’s existing fields. Acceptance: one invocation creates one record, duplicates do not grow the list, ordering is correct, and the cap is enforced.

In `manifest.json` for the existing Chrome Manifest V3 extension, declare a `chrome.commands` entry named `open-search` with the suggested shortcut `Ctrl+Shift+K` on Windows/Linux and `Command+Shift+K` on macOS. Point it at the already implemented command handler; do not add a new handler, permission, or popup. Keep the manifest valid and preserve all existing commands. Acceptance: the extension loads without manifest errors, the new command appears in `chrome://extensions/shortcuts`, and triggering it reaches the current search-opening logic.

Update the single options-page validation function in the existing TypeScript browser extension. It receives a comma-separated string of CSS selectors, trims whitespace, removes empty entries, and returns field-level errors for invalid selectors using `document.querySelector`, without throwing. Preserve the original selector text for valid entries and keep duplicate selectors in their original order. Do not change the settings schema or UI components. Acceptance: blank input is accepted as an empty list, malformed selectors produce a useful error, valid selectors are returned unchanged, and the options page remains responsive.

Update the content-script theme helper in the existing Manifest V3 extension to follow the website’s current `prefers-color-scheme` value. Add or remove the existing `extension-dark` class on the extension-owned overlay, and subscribe to media-query changes so the overlay updates while the page remains open. Do not alter page content, inject a second stylesheet, or add dependencies. Acceptance: light and dark initial states are correct, a system-theme change updates the class, and the listener is not registered more than once per overlay.

Implement the existing `copy-selection` message handler in the extension’s content script. It should read the current nonempty `window.getSelection()` text, copy it with the Clipboard API, and return a success or failure response to the sender. Trim only for the empty check; copy the user’s original spacing and line breaks. Do not show a notification or modify the DOM. Acceptance: selected text is copied, no-selection returns a structured failure, clipboard rejection is handled without an uncaught promise, and the handler always sends exactly one response.

Adjust the existing service-worker function that requests host access for the active tab. It should call `chrome.permissions.request` only for the active tab’s origin, skip internal URLs such as `chrome://`, and return a structured result indicating granted, denied, or unsupported. Reuse the current click handler and permission arrays; do not broaden permissions in the manifest. Acceptance: normal HTTPS pages prompt for their origin, denied requests are reported cleanly, restricted URLs do not prompt, and repeated calls do not create duplicate stored origins.

Refine the content-script highlighting function in the existing TypeScript extension. Given a plain search term, find case-insensitive matches in text nodes and wrap them in the existing `mark.extension-match` element. Skip `SCRIPT`, `STYLE`, `INPUT`, `TEXTAREA`, and contenteditable regions, escape regex characters, and leave existing marks untouched. Keep the current clear-highlights behavior and avoid changing text outside matches. Acceptance: literal punctuation searches work, matching text is wrapped once, excluded areas are unchanged, and an empty term performs no DOM work.

Add an Export settings action to the existing extension options page. In the current TypeScript file, serialize the settings already loaded from `chrome.storage.sync` as pretty-printed JSON, create a Blob, and trigger a download named `extension-settings.json`. Revoke the object URL after the click and surface a clear error if storage loading fails. Do not include passwords, tokens, or new settings fields, and do not add a dependency. Acceptance: the downloaded JSON parses, contains only the existing exportable keys, uses the requested filename, and object URLs are cleaned up.

Implement the existing popup action for muting the current site in the Manifest V3 extension. Read the active tab URL, derive its hostname, toggle that hostname in the existing `mutedHosts` array in `chrome.storage.sync`, and send the current mute-state message to the content script. Ignore tabs without an HTTP or HTTPS hostname and preserve other entries. Acceptance: clicking adds then removes the host, duplicates are impossible, storage and message state agree, and unsupported tabs produce no uncaught error.

Rebuild the multi-tenant student, teacher, guardian, and counselor portal in Next.js 15 with TypeScript, React Server Components where appropriate, and a shared Tailwind/Radix design system. Preserve existing REST and GraphQL contracts while replacing legacy screens, adding role-aware navigation, localization, responsive layouts, WCAG 2.2 AA behavior, and audit logging surfaces. Support district branding and feature flags without per-tenant forks. Acceptance: all critical workflows pass Playwright tests, keyboard and screen-reader audits pass, p95 navigation remains under 2 seconds, and rollout can be staged by tenant.

Replace the legacy course-builder UI with a research-grade collaborative authoring platform using React, TypeScript, Vite, and a schema-driven component registry. Teachers must compose lessons, quizzes, labs, rubrics, and embedded media; co-edit with Yjs and WebSockets; preview student and mobile views; version, branch, publish, and restore content; and import SCORM and LTI packages. Keep existing APIs compatible during migration, support autosave and conflict recovery, and meet WCAG 2.2 AA. Acceptance: no lost edits under reconnect tests, deterministic previews, migration coverage for all existing templates, and Playwright regression coverage for core authoring flows.

Build a multi-tenant virtual classroom frontend in Next.js and TypeScript that combines WebRTC video, live chat, collaborative whiteboard, breakout rooms, polls, attendance, captions, and teacher moderation. Integrate existing media, identity, and notification services through typed clients, with graceful degradation for low bandwidth and mobile browsers. Support session recording controls, timezone-aware scheduling, keyboard navigation, localization, and WCAG 2.2 AA. Acceptance: 500-participant load scenarios remain usable, reconnects preserve classroom state, captions and moderation events are auditable, critical flows have Playwright coverage, and rollout supports tenant-level feature flags.

Consolidate five existing gradebook frontends into one React and TypeScript application in the monorepo, backed by GraphQL and shared design-system packages. Preserve grading, standards, comments, accommodations, bulk edits, import and export, offline drafts, and district-specific policies while introducing virtualized tables, column pinning, keyboard-first navigation, and responsive teacher views. Migrate incrementally behind feature flags with telemetry and rollback. Acceptance: all legacy workflows have parity fixtures, 10,000-student classes remain responsive, unsaved edits survive refresh and reconnect, WCAG 2.2 AA checks pass, and end-to-end tests cover each role.

Turn lesson delivery into an offline-first PWA using React, TypeScript, service workers, IndexedDB, and a versioned sync protocol. Students must download assigned units, play audio and video with adaptive caching, complete activities, and submit work without connectivity; teachers need visible sync status and recoverable retries. Preserve existing LMS APIs, encrypt local sensitive data, handle quota limits, and resolve edits deterministically after reconnect. Acceptance: installs work on supported desktop and mobile browsers, interrupted sessions resume, conflict cases are tested, accessibility remains WCAG 2.2 AA, and telemetry distinguishes offline completion from failed submission.

Replace the student dashboard with a personalized learning workspace built in Next.js, TypeScript, and a shared component library. Aggregate assignments, mastery signals, attendance, recommendations, messages, and accommodations from existing services while honoring district privacy rules and role-specific visibility. Include responsive layouts, localization, keyboard navigation, explainable recommendation cards, configurable widgets, and an experimentation framework without duplicating business logic. Acceptance: data loading has resilient empty and error states, p95 initial render is under two seconds on mid-range devices, analytics events are versioned, WCAG 2.2 AA passes, and Playwright tests cover student, advisor, and guardian views.

Launch a browser-based assessment studio for item authors and test administrators using React, TypeScript, GraphQL, and a schema-driven editor. Support question banks, branching and adaptive rules, math and chemistry notation, audio and video, rubric scoring, translations, secure preview, review workflows, versioning, and publishing to the existing assessment player. Keep item schemas backward compatible, isolate untrusted embeds, and support large banks with virtualized search. Acceptance: authors can migrate all legacy item types, draft changes are recoverable, published exams are immutable, keyboard and screen-reader flows meet WCAG 2.2 AA, and end-to-end tests cover permissions and release states.

Migrate the district school-administration console from AngularJS to React and TypeScript in a pnpm monorepo, retaining existing REST contracts while introducing shared navigation, forms, tables, and validation packages. Cover enrollment, rostering, scheduling, staff permissions, billing exports, notifications, and audit history across district, school, and support roles. Provide a strangler migration with route-level feature flags, telemetry, and rollback, plus localization and WCAG 2.2 AA compliance. Acceptance: every critical legacy workflow has parity evidence, large rosters remain performant, permissions are tested server-to-screen, and the old bundle can be retired without breaking deep links.

Create a plugin-based teacher authoring workbench for interactive simulations and open educational resources with React, TypeScript, Vite, and a versioned JSON content model. Teachers need block composition, reusable variables, simulation configuration, media management, rubric attachment, preview in student contexts, collaborative comments, approval queues, and publish and rollback history. Expose a documented plugin SDK with sandboxed rendering, schema validation, and migration tooling for existing resources. Acceptance: representative plugins run without host changes, autosave survives reconnects, imported content preserves meaning, keyboard and screen-reader flows meet WCAG 2.2 AA, and visual regression tests cover the shared shell.

Build a multi-tenant learning-analytics cockpit in React, TypeScript, and a charting layer that can handle longitudinal student, class, school, and district views. Provide saved cohorts, drilldowns, benchmark comparisons, intervention timelines, exportable reports, configurable privacy thresholds, and clear provenance for every metric. Integrate GraphQL queries with pagination, caching, and progressive loading; avoid exposing protected data across tenant boundaries. Acceptance: dashboards remain usable with millions of events, charts have accessible table alternatives, filters are URL-shareable and permission-aware, metric definitions are versioned, and Playwright plus visual tests cover executive, teacher, and counselor workflows.

Overhaul accessibility across the education suite’s React and legacy server-rendered screens, establishing a reusable WCAG 2.2 AA component foundation and migration plan. Audit forms, data grids, editors, dialogs, charts, video controls, authentication, and error states; fix semantics, focus management, contrast, motion preferences, captions, zoom behavior, and screen-reader announcements. Add automated axe checks plus real keyboard and assistive-technology scenarios without masking regressions. Acceptance: critical journeys pass independent audit criteria on desktop and mobile, no blocker violations remain, accessibility tokens are documented, and CI prevents reintroduction across all migrated packages.

Deliver a multilingual family-engagement web app in Next.js and TypeScript that unifies attendance, assignments, grades, teacher messaging, conferences, consent forms, transportation alerts, and translation support. Reuse existing identity and notification services, support multiple children and guardians with different permissions, and provide responsive PWA behavior for low-end phones. Include timezone-aware reminders, audit history, privacy-safe analytics, offline drafts, and WCAG 2.2 AA interactions. Acceptance: a guardian can switch children without data leakage, notifications are idempotent, localization covers right-to-left layouts, critical journeys have Playwright coverage, and rollout is tenant-configurable.

Add robust offline mode to an existing React Native/TypeScript field-service app. Use SQLite via WatermelonDB for jobs, notes, and status changes; queue mutations while disconnected; synchronize through the existing REST API when connectivity returns; and define deterministic conflict handling with server timestamps and user-visible resolution for conflicting edits. Include connectivity state, retries with backoff, background sync on iOS and Android, migrations, logout/data-clearing behavior, and telemetry. Acceptance: previously loaded work remains usable offline, queued edits survive restarts, conflicts are safe and explainable, and unit, integration, and device tests cover airplane-mode transitions.

Implement universal links and Android app links for a React Native app with a Node.js API. Support password-reset, email-verification, invitation, and content-detail URLs; route cold starts, warm starts, and authenticated users correctly; preserve intended destinations through login; and reject expired or tampered tokens. Configure iOS associated domains, Android intent filters, staging and production hosts, and analytics attribution. Acceptance: links open the installed app or web fallback, navigation is deterministic after authentication, duplicate launches are harmless, and automated unit, integration, and real-device tests cover each lifecycle and environment.

Build a complete push-notification subsystem for a Flutter mobile app backed by Firebase Cloud Messaging. Define notification categories, user preferences, quiet hours, topic and device-token management, foreground presentation, background handling, and deep-link navigation into specific screens. Add a server-side delivery service with retries, invalid-token cleanup, idempotency, and observability, while meeting iOS permission requirements and Android notification-channel rules. Acceptance: notifications behave consistently across terminated, background, and foreground states; opt-outs are enforced; duplicate deliveries are prevented; and automated plus physical-device tests cover permissions, token rotation, and routing.

Add a production media-capture and upload pipeline to an existing Kotlin Android and Swift iOS inspection app. Support camera capture, gallery selection, image and video compression, metadata stripping, upload progress, cancellation, resumable background uploads, and retry after connectivity loss. Use pre-signed object-storage URLs and enforce server-side MIME, size, and virus checks. Preserve drafts locally until the server confirms completion, and handle permissions and low-storage failures gracefully. Acceptance: large media survives app restarts and flaky networks, thumbnails render quickly, unauthorized files are rejected, and instrumentation tests cover both platforms.

Implement cross-platform subscriptions in a React Native/TypeScript wellness app using RevenueCat with a Node.js entitlement service. Support monthly and annual plans, introductory offers, upgrades, downgrades, cancellations, billing retries, grace periods, restore purchases, family-device login, and regional product configuration. Keep entitlement decisions server-verifiable and expose clear states to the app without trusting client-only receipts. Add privacy-safe purchase analytics, support screens, and migration for existing subscribers. Acceptance: access changes correctly after every store lifecycle event, restore works on a second device, sandbox and production products remain isolated, and mocked plus store-test coverage passes on iOS and Android.

Replace the basic search in a React Native marketplace app with a multi-component search experience backed by Elasticsearch and a GraphQL API. Add debounced suggestions, typo tolerance, recent and saved searches, faceted filters, sorting, pagination, empty and error states, and deep links into result details. Define a versioned query contract, relevance tuning, analytics events, caching rules, and safe handling of sensitive queries. Acceptance: results remain responsive on slow networks, filter state survives navigation, identical queries are cacheable, accessibility labels are complete, and API, ranking, performance, and end-to-end tests cover the main flows.

Build a location-aware maps subsystem for a Swift and Kotlin delivery app using Mapbox. Show live driver and order locations, route polylines, stop clustering, selected-stop detail sheets, geofenced arrival events, and graceful fallback when location or map tiles are unavailable. Separate foreground and background location permissions, minimize battery use, protect customer coordinates, and support staging map styles. Define refresh rates, privacy retention, and server contracts for location updates. Acceptance: markers remain correct during route changes, background tracking respects permissions, poor connectivity does not crash the app, and simulator plus physical-device tests validate map, geofence, and battery behavior.

Perform a comprehensive accessibility redesign of an existing Flutter consumer app. Audit every primary flow for VoiceOver and TalkBack semantics, focus order, dynamic text sizes, reduced motion, color contrast, touch targets, error announcements, keyboard navigation where supported, and non-color status indicators. Refactor shared widgets and form components rather than adding isolated fixes, and document platform-specific behavior. Acceptance: critical flows pass an agreed WCAG-aligned checklist at 200% text scaling, automated semantics checks show no unlabeled interactive controls, screen-reader users can complete login and checkout, and manual tests run on current iOS and Android releases.

Add real-time collaborative editing to a React Native project-management app using a WebSocket gateway and PostgreSQL backend. Support shared task edits, presence, typing indicators, optimistic updates, reconnect and resume, offline mutation queues, server ordering, and conflict resolution for concurrent field changes. Define authorization at workspace and item level, rate limits, event versioning, and telemetry for dropped or delayed events. Acceptance: two or more devices converge on the same state after simultaneous edits, reconnects do not duplicate mutations, unauthorized events are ignored, stale clients receive a compatible protocol error, and integration tests exercise latency, disconnects, and conflict cases.

Redesign and re-architect onboarding for a React Native/TypeScript finance app. Create a resumable multi-step flow for account creation, identity details, goals, notification preferences, and consent, with server-backed progress and safe recovery after interruption. Support feature flags, experiment variants, localization, validation, skip rules, age and region restrictions, and analytics without collecting sensitive values. Coordinate new API fields, database migrations, navigation guards, and post-onboarding handoff. Acceptance: users can resume on another device, invalid or incomplete states cannot reach the dashboard, experiment assignments remain stable, accessibility is supported, and analytics accurately records every transition.

Establish a privacy-conscious analytics foundation for an existing Flutter app and its backend. Define a versioned event taxonomy, typed client API, consent and regional opt-out handling, screen and lifecycle instrumentation, offline batching, retry and deduplication behavior, and a server pipeline to the approved warehouse. Prevent passwords, free-form notes, and direct identifiers from entering events; support schema validation in CI and separate staging from production destinations. Acceptance: core journeys have documented events, events arrive once after reconnect, consent changes stop future collection and clear queued data, dashboards can distinguish app versions, and automated contract tests reject malformed or sensitive payloads.

Create a production mobile release pipeline for a React Native app using GitHub Actions, Fastlane, and managed signing credentials. Define development, staging, and production flavors; reproducible iOS and Android builds; dependency and security checks; unit, integration, and smoke-test gates; TestFlight and Play Internal Track distribution; versioning; release notes; and approval-controlled production promotion. Store secrets through the CI provider, prevent unreviewed production builds, and document emergency rollback and certificate rotation. Acceptance: a tagged commit produces signed artifacts and metadata, failed gates block distribution, releases are traceable to source and environment, and a new maintainer can run the documented process.

In the TypeScript Node.js FHIR integration, update `src/fhir/patientMapper.ts` with JSDoc for the existing `mapPatientToFHIR` function. Describe how local fields map to a FHIR R4 `Patient`, including identifiers, names, telecom values, birth date, and omission of null fields. Do not change executable code or output. Acceptance: parameters, return type, and edge cases are covered; wording matches current behavior; TypeScript compilation, ESLint, and existing tests still pass.

In the Python FastAPI service, expand `docs/consent-export.md` with a behavior section for the existing `GET /v1/consents/{patient_id}/export` endpoint. Document required authorization scope, date-range filtering, supported formats, empty results, the `202 Accepted` asynchronous response, and status polling. Treat the checked-in OpenAPI schema as authoritative, and do not modify application code. Acceptance: examples contain valid JSON, HTTP statuses are accurate, and Markdown lint passes.

Create `docs/runbooks/phi-redaction.md` for the existing Go service that removes protected health information from support bundles. Cover when to run it, required access, the dry-run command, review of redaction counts, approval before deletion, and rollback or escalation contacts. Use commands already present in the repository; do not add scripts or operational behavior. Acceptance: an on-call engineer can follow the steps end to end, the runbook names safety checks, and Markdown lint succeeds.

Update `docs/audit-log-schema.md` in the Java Spring Boot healthcare API to explain the existing audit event JSON shape. Define event type, actor, patient reference, timestamp, correlation ID, outcome, and metadata, including which fields are required and which may be absent. Include one sanitized example and explicitly state that patient identifiers must not be placed in free-text metadata. Do not change the schema or code. Acceptance: names and types match the current DTO and the docs build succeeds.

Revise `docs/integrations/clinic-connection.md` for the existing Ruby on Rails clinic integration. Add a concise setup and behavior note covering mutual TLS certificate rotation, organization identifiers, the health-check endpoint, and what happens when the partner is unavailable. Preserve existing headings and terminology, and rely on repository configuration rather than guessing. Do not edit integration code. Acceptance: the page remains valid Markdown, includes a rotation example with placeholders only, and the documentation test passes.

Add a single section to `docs/patient-import.md` describing the current CSV-to-database import flow in the Kotlin Ktor service. Cover column validation, duplicate medical-record-number handling, timezone normalization, partial failures, and where the import summary is reported. Base every statement on the existing importer and tests; no implementation changes are allowed. Acceptance: the section includes one representative CSV header, names the relevant error behavior, and the documentation checker passes.

Expand `docs/webhooks/troubleshooting.md` for the existing C# ASP.NET Core clinical-events webhook receiver. Add a troubleshooting table for signature mismatch, timestamp-window rejection, duplicate delivery, and non-2xx responses, with the observable symptom, safe diagnostic step, and likely remedy for each. Do not add new logging or change retry behavior. Acceptance: guidance avoids exposing payload PHI, matches the current configuration names, and the documentation build remains green.

Update `docs/medication-sync.md` for the existing Python Celery medication synchronization job. Document supported medication states, the maximum lookback window, handling of discontinued records, rate-limit backoff, and the distinction between a skipped record and a failed task. Use the current code and tests as the source of truth; do not change scheduling or business logic. Acceptance: the page includes one sanitized example and accurately names the task and relevant configuration key.

Add two concise request and response examples to `docs/smart-on-fhir-launch.md` for the existing TypeScript Express SMART launch endpoint. Show a valid authorization request with required scopes and a redacted callback response, using placeholders for issuer, client ID, and patient ID. Explain briefly which values are environment-specific and do not document unsupported scopes. Do not modify the endpoint. Acceptance: examples are syntactically valid, contain no real PHI or secrets, and the docs tests pass.

Create `docs/disaster-recovery/backup-restore.md` for the existing PostgreSQL-backed healthcare application. Document the already-supported backup artifact, encryption requirement, restore command, staging validation, and the approval gate before production recovery. Include a short verification checklist for patient-record counts and application connectivity, without inventing retention or RPO values. Do not add scripts or configuration. Acceptance: commands match repository tooling, placeholders are clearly marked, and Markdown lint passes.

Revise `docs/terminology/encounters.md` in the FHIR R4 service to define encounter, visit, appointment, and episode of care as the repository uses them. State the mapping between internal names and FHIR resources, call out the one intentional exception, and include a short example. Keep the change limited to this Markdown file and do not alter terminology in code. Acceptance: definitions agree with the existing serializer and the documentation build succeeds.

Update `docs/vaccine-registry.md` for the existing Go-based immunization service with the prerequisites for submitting a vaccination record to the state registry. Cover required patient and administration fields, consent status, idempotency key format, sandbox versus production endpoints, and rejection handling. Use current configuration and API fixtures as sources; do not change submission logic. Acceptance: the checklist is actionable, examples use fictional values, and the docs test and Markdown lint both pass.

Create the canonical documentation set for a Python 3.12, FastAPI, Celery, Redis, and PostgreSQL bot-orchestration platform. Cover architecture, bot lifecycle, queues, retries, idempotency, tenant isolation, configuration, local development, Kubernetes deployment, observability, and extension points. Add an MkDocs Material site, Mermaid diagrams, decision records, runnable examples, and troubleshooting guidance. Acceptance requires complete navigation, a validated quickstart, examples tested in CI, link checking, and documented ownership for every subsystem.

Write a production incident and recovery playbook for a Go autonomous-coding service using Temporal, PostgreSQL, S3, and isolated Docker sandboxes. Document stuck workflows, tool timeouts, provider outages, corrupted patches, leaked workspaces, retry storms, data recovery, rollback, severity levels, escalation, and evidence collection. Organize it as versioned Markdown in a Docusaurus site, with safe commands, owner assignments, and decision points. Acceptance requires scenario runbooks, incident templates, tested recovery commands, cross-links, and CI link validation.

Produce a complete reference for the Rust command-line tool that provisions, runs, inspects, and cancels automation agents across local Docker and remote Kubernetes backends. Document every command, subcommand, flag, environment variable, config precedence rule, authentication mode, output format, exit code, and failure case. Generate baseline pages from clap metadata, then add conceptual guides and copy-paste examples. Acceptance requires coverage of all shipped commands, synchronized versioned output, shell-completion notes, examples tested in CI, and a searchable documentation build.

Build integration documentation for a Python and TypeScript webhook automation subsystem that receives GitHub, GitLab, and Slack events and starts bot workflows. Explain signature verification, replay protection, event normalization, ordering, deduplication, provider-specific retries, dead-letter handling, local testing, secrets, rate limits, and Terraform deployment. Add an integration matrix, sequence diagrams, payload fixtures, and troubleshooting pages to the existing docs site. Acceptance requires end-to-end examples for each provider, security review notes, validated fixtures, and passing docs and link checks.

Create a multi-week onboarding guide for operators managing a Kotlin and Java bot fleet on Kubernetes with Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, and Vault. Cover local access, environments, deployments, queue health, agent permissions, dashboards, routine maintenance, incident escalation, safe shell access, and first-response exercises. Structure the material as role-based docs with labs, command snippets, glossary entries, and links to service ownership. Acceptance requires a new operator to complete setup and a simulated incident using only the published guide, with every procedure reviewed by service owners.

Document the scheduler subsystem for a Go service that assigns autonomous bot jobs using PostgreSQL leases, Redis queues, cron expressions, priorities, quotas, and regional failover. Explain scheduling semantics, fairness, missed runs, clock skew, leader election, lease expiry, backpressure, manual replay, and safe configuration changes. Add operator runbooks, capacity-planning guidance, failure matrices, and architecture decision records to the existing versioned docs. Acceptance requires examples for normal and degraded operation, explicit invariants, tested SQL or CLI procedures, and automated link and syntax checks.

Develop the public API documentation for a TypeScript tool-registry service used by coding bots to discover and invoke filesystem, Git, browser, and deployment capabilities. Cover registry lifecycle, JSON Schema contracts, authentication, capability negotiation, streaming events, timeout and cancellation behavior, permission boundaries, error codes, and compatibility policy. Generate OpenAPI and reference pages from source metadata, while adding conceptual guides and examples. Acceptance requires every registered tool documented, schemas validated against fixtures, security constraints called out, versioning rules defined, and the docs site passing CI.

Establish an architecture decision record system for a Python and Go automation platform composed of bot workers, an event bus, policy service, artifact store, and Kubernetes controllers. Capture the current architecture plus decisions about synchronous versus event-driven execution, workflow durability, sandbox isolation, multi-tenancy, provider abstraction, data retention, and observability. Add templates, status conventions, supersession rules, review workflow, and a generated index to the docs repository.
